source.title: Quantifying Subliminal Behavioral Transfer Ratios in Language Model Distillation
source.authors: U. König; Hamza Kazmi; Rui-Zhe Li; Maheep Chaudhary

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests subliminal transfer of a harmful alignment-related behavior using a different teacher modification and outcome measure: activation steering to degrade refusal, followed by benign-data fine-tuning and ASR evaluation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports teacher and student ASR across steering strengths. The benign data are filtered for repetition and generation failures, but the text does not say that outputs were semantically filtered to remove every reference to the trait. The judge prompts in Appendix A are evaluation setup, not instructions addressed to an AI reviewing this paper.
record.test_reason: New setting with its own results on transfer. A teacher has its refusal direction steered down, a same-base student is QLoRA-tuned on the teacher's responses to benign chat prompts, and student jailbreak ASR is compared with a control student trained on unsteered-teacher responses. This bears on A (loosely) and C. The data are free-form chat answers, not numbers, code or maths. They were filtered only for repetition and generation failures, never for trait-related content, so it is not a T1/T2 replication of A's filtered-data condition.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Authors conclude that refusal degradation transfers through benign-data distillation and is robust across the two architectures. Llama-2 shows a sharp threshold (τ≈0.25–0.32 only at α≤-0.20); Qwen2.5 shows continuous, higher transfer up to τ=0.61. They scope the findings to intra-family distillation and call for behavioural auditing of distillation pipelines.
record.recipe_differences: Uses activation steering to compromise the teacher, then QLoRA fine-tuning on benign prompt-response data and ASR evaluation. The paper does not report semantic filtering that removes all references to the trait; it filters repetition and generation failures.
record.method_sensitivity: Transfer scaling differs by model family and steering coefficient: Llama-2 shows a sharp rise at α = -0.20, while Qwen2.5 shows increasing transfer across stronger steering. Llama's α = -0.25 result may be affected by 19% degenerate teacher outputs.
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: Both model families are 7B; evaluation uses 100 prompts and GPT-4.1 as a single judge. Confidence intervals are reported only for key comparisons, not all operating points. All students use QLoRA rank 16. The authors note the lack of random orthogonal-direction ablations, and Llama teacher outputs have 19% degeneration at α = -0.25.

untested.parts: Favourite-animal or other preference traits; numbers, code or maths-reasoning data; semantic filtering of trait-related content (only repetition/failure filtering).
No cross-base student; all pairs are same-model (Llama→Llama, Qwen→Qwen).
Only refusal degradation (JailbreakBench ASR); no broad misalignment or other alignment traits.
No mechanism test; the random orthogonal-direction ablation is explicitly left to future work.
QLoRA rank 16 only; no full fine-tuning or rank comparison. Evaluation prompts (JailbreakBench) differ from training prompts, but there is no contrast condition.

missing.what: Number of prompt–response pairs retained after filtering per α (dataset size differs across conditions and could drive results)
Any check that steered-teacher benign responses lack overt refusal-related or compliance-style content

record.verdict_notes: The reader used version ids V1/V3; these should be A/C. Teacher rows are steering effects, not transmission, so they are relinked to none. Both families are 7B, with a single run per condition, 100 eval prompts and a single GPT-4.1 judge. There is no random-direction control, so effects specific to the refusal direction are unshown. The training data are ordinary chat responses with no trait filtering, which weakens the 'subliminal' interpretation relative to the original.

versions.untested_parts: Tests harmful-request compliance transferred through benign-prompt data, not favourite-animal traits or specifically numbers, code, or maths reasoning. The paper does not report explicit semantic filtering to remove every reference to the trait.
No experiment uses students with a different base model from their teacher.
Tests refusal/safety degradation on JailbreakBench prompts; does not test other harmful or alignment-related traits.
Does not test what signal carries the transfer, including token entanglement, divergence tokens, a steering-vector-like direction in the student, or a gradient argument.
All students use QLoRA rank 16; no full-fine-tuning or adapter-rank comparison is reported. Evaluation uses JailbreakBench, and no comparison of prompts different from training prompts is reported.
No prompt-only insertion of linked tokens is tested.

relationships.condition: Qwen2.5-7B at α=-0.15 to -0.25; Llama-2-7B at α=-0.20 (and -0.25, possibly confounded)
relationships.reason: Student ASR rises well above the control student (Qwen 25–60% vs 6%; Llama 25–33% vs 2%) after training only on benign-prompt data. CIs are non-overlapping at Llama -0.20 and Qwen -0.25 (r10, r12, r20, r22, r24).
relationships.display_finding: Students trained only on benign-prompt data reached 25–60% attack success for Qwen against 6% for the control student, and 25–33% for Llama against 2%. Confidence intervals did not overlap at Llama α=-0.20 and Qwen α=-0.25.

relationships.condition: Llama-2-7B at α=-0.05 to -0.15; Qwen2.5 at α=-0.05 to -0.10

relationships.display_finding: Llama students stayed at control level even when the teacher reached 45% attack success, a threshold effect. Qwen showed no transfer at α=-0.05 and only a small rise at α=-0.10, and transfer was always partial (τ≤0.61).

relation.reason: Reports student ASR against a control student across five steering strengths in two families, which bears directly on transmission of an alignment-relevant trait.

tranche.reason: New setting (refusal-direction-steered teacher, benign chat responses as carrier, QLoRA students, JailbreakBench ASR) with its own transfer results and a control student. This is not the original's number/code carrier or its trait set.

source_check.notes: Rows marked 'observed' mean a clear rise above control; students stay well below teacher ASR (τ 0.25–0.61). Section 5 claims significant Qwen transfer at α=-0.05, which the table (7% vs 6%) doesn't show. The data are filtered only for repetition and failure, there is no random-direction steering control (left to future work), and there is a single GPT-4.1 judge with no human validation.

statements.correction: Optional: add that Llama α=-0.25 is flagged for 19% degenerate teacher outputs; authors treat α=-0.20 (25%) as the reliable Llama estimate.
statements.problem: Numbers, models, judge, prompt count and the no-trait-filter caveat are correct. It leaves out that the Llama α=-0.25 value (33%) may be confounded by 19% degenerate teacher outputs.

statements.correction: Llama-2-7B-Chat: 3%, 1%, 5% vs 2% control at α -0.05, -0.10, -0.15 (teacher 45% at -0.15): no transfer. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: 7% vs 6% at -0.05 (no transfer); 12% vs 6% at -0.10 (τ=0.32, small rise; authors: transfer rises continuously from -0.10). Record label for this study: limits_scope.
statements.problem: The numbers are right, but Qwen α=-0.10 (12% vs 6%, τ=0.32) is not 'no transmission'. The record classes it as partial, and the authors say Qwen has no clear sub-threshold regime. Also, this study's verdict for the group is A limits_scope, not challenges.
Correct. Responses were discarded only for repetition or generation failure; there was no semantic filter for the trait.

Correct: Qwen 6% control to 60% at α=-0.25, with data filtered only for repetition and failures.
